title: Session degradation triage — idea pad
content:
Context and motivation:

- We currently have several fallback mechanisms when tokens/latency/cost spike: model downgrade, truncated context, and timeouts that surface to the client. But we have no single lightweight triage layer that tries fast, conservative remediations in a prioritized order before exposing a hard failure to the app.
- Goal: define a small, testable "session degradation triage" feature that sits between request admission and final fallback. It should perform quick, low-risk interventions to keep user-facing flows alive and within SLOs.

High-level idea (one-liner):
- A prioritized, configurable triage pipeline for each session that attempts incremental, measurable degradations (cheap -> moderate -> heavy) with telemetry hooks and safety checks.

Why this matters:
- Improves perceived reliability without requiring heavy-handed global fallbacks.
- Saves tokens/cost by avoiding immediate full model fallbacks for recoverable spikes.
- Gives product teams deterministic knobs and observability for graceful degradation strategies.

Target users and scenarios:
- Chatbots with long histories where occasional long-turn inputs increase latency/cost.
- Enterprise customers on Dedicated with strict 95th percentile latency SLOs.
- Mobile apps with flaky networks where tail latency matters.

Proposed triage actions (ordered by aggressiveness):
1) Lightweight local actions (sub-second):
   - Soft length clamp: apply a mild early token limit for the *current request* if estimated token count > threshold.
   - Prefix skip heuristics: drop low-value system or assistant tokens that match configured anchors (e.g., verbose debug prompts).
2) Cache-aware actions (few ms):
   - Prefer cached KV prefixes (if near-match) and short-circuit generation with cached continuations when similarity > X.
   - Switch to cached prompt templates for repeated user intents.
3) Model variant shift (tens of ms + potential cost savings):
   - Try lower-cost quantized variant with same architecture for remainder of session.
   - If model variant doesn't exist, try shorter context lengths with same model.
4) Response shaping / synthesis (moderate):
   - Return a concise summary instead of full generation (auto-abbreviate large outputs).
   - Use structured response with placeholders + post-hoc fetch for details (deferred fetch).
5) Last-resort fallback (heavy):
   - Hard truncate context and continue.
   - Return an explicit degraded response (toast to user: "temporarily shortened for speed").

User stories (initial):
- As an engineer, I want a per-session priority policy so I can tune how aggressive triage is for power users vs casual users.
- As a product manager, I want telemetry showing which triage action was applied and its effect on latency/cost so I can make tradeoffs.
- As an SRE, I want triage to be opt-in by route and observable in Console with per-action metrics and traces.

Acceptance criteria (MVP):
- Configurable triage pipeline enabled on a route-level, with 3 ordered actions (soft clamp, cache-pref, model-variant try).
- Telemetry events emitted for each attempted action with outcome and delta on latency and token usage.
- Safety: no action should silently change user-visible semantics (unless route configured to allow explicit degraded messaging).
- Integration tests that simulate token surge and assert that triage lowered tail latency in >80% of trials.

Data/metrics to capture:
- pre-action estimated tokens, post-action actual tokens, tokens saved
- latency at p50/p95/p99 for requests with triage vs control
- success rate per action (e.g., cache-hit avoided fallback)
- cost delta estimate per session

Design considerations / open questions:
- How to estimate "value" of context to decide what to drop? (heuristics vs learned scoring)
- Per-session state: store triage history to avoid flipping actions repeatedly (cooldown window?)
- Interaction with rollouts and Canary: should triage be applied differently for canary cohorts?
- Billing implications for enterprise: customers may want to opt out of auto-downgrades. Need per-tenant controls.

Quick experiment plan (phase 0):
- Synthetic load test: simulate sessions with long contexts and bursty request spikes. Compare baseline vs triage-enabled routes. Metrics: p95 latency and tokens.
- AB test on small percentage of traffic with opt-in flag. Collect telemetry for 1 week.
- Qualitative: instrument a handful of customers to collect feedback when triage returned "degraded" responses.

Implementation notes (runtime):
- Keep triage code path minimal and in the admission layer to avoid adding new hop latencies.
- Leverage existing KV/caching infra and model variant metadata.
- Expose triage decisions in request-level trace/span for Console surface.

Risks and mitigations:
- User confusion if responses are silently shortened -> add opt-in header and clear degraded response field.
- Increased complexity on routing -> start with route opt-in, small set of actions, iterate.
- Wrong heuristics could harm quality -> add QA gate with prompt-based evals and allow quick rollback.

To-do (next 2 weeks):
- Draft a lightweight PRD (expand ACs and rollout plan) — assigned to me.
- Sync with Console owners to design telemetry schema. (Ava)
- Prototype soft clamp + cache-pref in local dev environment, add synthetic tests. (Zoe)
- Add Linear ticket and link runtime PR.

Notes to self:
- Keep triage decisions explainable in logs. Avoid ML-only blackbox scoring for MVP.
- Consider fraction-based rollout by route and by tenant size.
- Touch base with legal for messaging requirements for enterprise customers.

Fragments/brainstorm snippets (random):
- "graceful degradation vector" idea: store brief canned fallbacks per integration so users get continuity instead of an error.
- Could surface a small "why shortened" token in response metadata for UX teams to show unobtrusive hints.
- Think about a "degradation budget" per session per day to limit how much we auto-shortened content.

-- end --
